utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are, with the Cymbeline radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: "The evidence from the Cymbeline radar was used by the HQ UNPROFOR G2 staff to ascertain the firing range of the mortars." At the time of the firing incident which happened on the 28th August, 1995, the radar was in operation on a direction arc and at an elevation that would have detected the trajectory of any mortar fired at a range of 950 metres or less: "Analysis showed that a round fired from 900 metres would have reached a vertex height on its trajectory, which would have been registered on the radar beam. The assessment was that the mortars were fired at a lower trajectory which passed under the radar beam. Any round fired at such a trajectory to pass under the radar beam would have come from a firing position, dependent on the charge, at a range between 1550 to 3500 [Realtime transcript read in error "5300"] metres. The difference of the confrontation line from the impact point is 1050 metres." Do you agree with these UNPROFOR findings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do is take what he said here in this report, as I am not a Cymbeline expert. So I have to take what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have to correct one number in the transcript. Page 39, line 7, "1550," sorry, "to" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even without not being an expert, do you find any contradictions in these findings? Because it says here for that radar -- that radar could have registered the trajectory of any shell that would have been fired at a distance of 250 metres or less?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 950, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 950 metres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And would it have been possibly easier to establish or determine the direction of a mortar that had come from a higher elevation and a further distance, in your view, if a shell was fired from 2400 metres under any angle with a charge that could have reached Markale, could have passed under the radar beam, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I don't have the technical information on how the Cymbeline was set up on this particular day. It could have been set up just looking at a particular area, so I find it very difficult to answer the question because I don't have the technical knowledge or how they were set upon this particular day to give you a definitive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you analyse this conclusion reached by UNPROFOR? Did you accept it? Did you reject it? And did this conclusion make it into your report and into your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used this report just as one of the background pieces of information to try and come to a -- an informed conclusion in my report. Whereas, it says here that they were aiming the Cymbeline to pick up obviously the mortars fired at the short ranges of 950 metres with a -- would have picked it up. That is one of the ranges the mortar could have been fired from. So I use this report then to remove that range from one of the possible ideas. So I did use this report just to help me in trying to reduce the options down of where the mortar could have been fired from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if I may just ask a question for my own clarification. I'm not sure whether to ask it to the witness because he said he doesn't know anything about Cymbeline radars, but I'm putting the question on the record nonetheless. The last sentence of this paragraph that we read says: "The distance to the confrontation line from the impact point is 1050 metres." Now, is it the distance from the front -- confrontation line that we need to look at, or is it the distance of the 2400 metres that we're looking at, which should fall between 1050 and 3500? I thought we're talking here about the distance from the firing point to Markale, not the distance from the confrontation line to Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, that we are discussing the firing point to Markale, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would be 2400 metres that we are working with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll work with a different distances, if you want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough. But if we are analysing whether a mortar fired from 2400 would have come below the radar or -- and be caught by the system or not, then we've got to put in 2400 here. And then, of course, we can put in any other number and, according to this formula, decide whether it would be below the radar or above the radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one more clarification, please. Did you establish whether the distance from Markale to the confrontation line was established correctly and that it was 1050 metres, or perhaps the confrontation line was at a distance of approximately 1950 metres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I had to use this time was the maps which I had been supplied which had the confrontation lines drawn on them. How accurate those lines are, obviously I don't know. So I was just basing it on the confrontation lines on those -- on the -- on the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And on those maps that you used, what was the distance of the confrontation line as it was marked on those maps, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can remember, it seemed to be between about 1200 and 1700 metres, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. You're familiar with the fact that both UNPROFOR members and investigation of the BiH established that due to the height of the building, the angle of descent should have been more than 67 degrees; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will go on using this information from now on. Did you analyse the firing tables that UNPROFOR used when coming up with their conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And using those same firing tables, were you able to verify the UNPROFOR findings and conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember if I was clarifying or supporting theirs. I use those tables then to come up with my own distances, which were here in the report. I can't remember if that confirms exactly with the other reports without re-reading them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now let's just briefly look at Eric Bleakely's statement, which is 1D1394. I am interested in page 10 in English and page 12 in B/C/S. As you can see, this is Mr. Eric Bleakely's statement. Somewhere in the middle, it says, "The tables give you ..." Mr. Bleakely explains the operation of a radar, and he says: "The tables give you the height with different charges. We combined this information with the ceiling of the Cymbeline radar, and I think that we came to two charges. The radar was looking at that part of the city. The second charge would have cut the beam. We then went to the Cymbeline radar. WO2 Andy Harris was the WO2 in charge of the facility. He took me to the back of the radar. I went with Powers. He showed me the arc on the map that the radar was looking at. At 170 degrees or 240 degrees ... the shell would have cut the beam. Gunner Rooney was the operator in the back of a vehicle. He was glued to the screen," as it were. And then looking at the same report, page 11 in English, paragraph 7. In B/C/S, this will be paragraph 5 on page 13. It says here: "I had the firing table for a Yugoslavia 120-millimetre mortar and I used them to calculate the maximum and minimum ranges." In other words, what he used for this analysis were the firing tables for a -- Yugoslavia 120-millimetre mortars. Did you find that to be correct as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you asking me to verify?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you also establish that UNPROFOR members, those who operated a Cymbeline radar, had the firing tables for a Yugoslavia 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know whether they did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We can see that Mr. Bleakely says here that with a different charge -- or, rather, the second charge would have cut the beam, according to Mr. Bleakely. In your report, you say that the first charge could have been used to fire at a distance of 900 metres from the point of impact, the second charge would have been 1600 from the point of impact, and that only the third charge could have propelled the shell to a distance of 2400 metres, and so on and so forth. We will come to the firing tables. Is it correct that Mr. Bleakely's findings were not incorporated in the comprehensive UN report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether these are in the comprehensive report or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just having trouble finding the reference to where Mr. Bleakely talks about it being fired from the second charge. If Mr. Lukic could please direct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry if it wasn't clear enough. It's English version of his statement, 1D1394. It's page 10. It's line 3 of the paragraph starting with, "Tables." It says: "The second charge would have cut the beam."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're using Mr. Bleakely's statement. I don't think it's in evidence at this moment. And if I read lines like: Angle of descent, I did not have the range tables with me but when I looked at the scene, I could not imagine the round coming in at that angle, et cetera. That, at least, asks for a further detailed analysis of this statement before we -- we take it as a statement of reference for what this witness tell us. We've struggled this morning with a lack of accurate measurements. Well, that -- these lines, and, of course, I have not seen the whole of the report, but ... it doesn't make me very optimistic about the accuracy of what that witness states.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up something that will clarify the matter in a more exact way. 1D1293. These are the firing tables for 120-millimetre mortar shells, and I believe that we have the document in the system. It used to be a 65 ter document, a Prosecutor's document. [In English] Yes. It's 65 ter 30261. Maybe it's better in fuller version with the translation. It's the first document from the list for this gentleman. [Interpretation] I know for a fact that in B/C/S I'm interested in page 57. [In English] I'm sorry, then we'll have to go back to the document I called first. It's 1D11293.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't this the document, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It should be the same document. But obviously the pages are not arranged the same way. Or at least the first one does not correspond with the line numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is the document that came after you asked for 1D1293 which you said is 30261, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it's in the system arranged the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The first document called up in B/C/S is the firing table for the 120-millimetre. The second one is an operations manual for that. I believe they're two different manuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Then it's not the same document. I misunderstood that it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, how about the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excellent idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of -- no, as a matter of fact, we are -- yes, we took the first break early as well. Let's stick to the -- as if Mr. Mladic would be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously I'm tuned up to that schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you need some time perhaps. Could the witness follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to raise a matter in relation to the scheduling of this witness, and we received a message from VWS. I think Mr. Higgs would very much like and would hope that the testimony could be concluded on Thursday. Now, in view of the time you've asked for, Mr. Lukic, that seems to be at least a bit problematic. Now, there are various solutions. One is that we say, Well, unfortunately we can't finish on Thursday. Another solution would be on the basis of a very accurate scheduling that by taking some extra time on Thursday we might be able to conclude, but that, of course, may meet objections by the Defence in view of Mr. Mladic's condition. Another option would be to nevertheless to sit tomorrow but then the Chamber already can tell you that we would only be able to sit 15 bis. The Chamber is open to accommodate the witness but sees all kinds of problems and invites the parties to give their views on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I would maybe ask the witness first, is it really necessary for him to leave? And if he says that it is, then we would rather -- because I have already one of my previous clients is testifying in Mr. Karadzic case and I'm visiting him tomorrow [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're not available for tomorrow. That's clear and is a good reason. Our scheduling order says that we're not sitting on this Wednesday. So, therefore, that's fully accepted. Then, extended time on Thursday might not help us out in view of your request to cross-examine the witness for eight hours which most likely effectively would have three and a half hours on Thursday. You used a little bit over two hours today. There's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two more hours, maybe more, three hours more. Two and a half hours [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be adjusted --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That would be the whole day, two sessions almost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll first inquire with the witness how compelling the reasons are and also tell him that we tried to accommodate him but that, until now, we see no possibility. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, you and I, we should not overlap, because the transcriber is missing all our important words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, before we continue, I'd like to inform you that we received a message from VWS whether there was any chance that we could complete your testimony by Thursday. Although all parties and the Chamber are quite willing to accommodate you, unfortunately, there are no possibilities for that and it is not to be expected that we could finish your examination by Thursday. We tried to do our best, but commitments elsewhere make it impossible, and we cannot sit for more than four days a week. I thank you for your understanding for the situation, because from your nodding yes, I understand that you accept that we cannot accommodate you. Mr. Lukic, could you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have on our screens now Mr. Higgs's report in both versions, since I was warned by them -- booths that they don't have this in front of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sure, it's P2605. We will need page 15 in English version, and page 23 in B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Higgs, I will first ask you to give me an explanation under letter (i), entitled: "Summary." In the second paragraph, it reads as follows, and I'm going to quote: "With a direction of 170 degrees and an angle of descent of approximately, it is possible to plot several locations of the origin of fire." Do you think that there is something missing here? What does this "approximately" mean and was it maybe just a typo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we had some small discretion with the angle of 67 to clear the building and another report said 70 degrees. It could also be I've had to approximate, therefore then, what ranges we may be able to achieve. So that's what I mean by the word "approximate."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] It says approximately.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You think 70 is missing maybe, 70 degrees?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Angle of approximately 70 degrees, it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the previous paragraphs -- paragraph you say: "The angle of descent, as suggested, was greater than 67 degrees and was probably nearer 70 degrees as explained in the report by the Bosnian authorities." So I don't know what your basis was for your -- later it says that an angle of approximately 70 degrees. So I take it that you took that as a starting point for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, who do you calculate on an approximate number? I mean, would then not be the outcome be approximately 900 metres or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What would be the difference if you start -- well, let's say, an angle of descent of 67 degrees compared to 72 degrees, what would be the difference in outcome approximately, as far as the distance of fire is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be dependant on what charge you're firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's start with charge 3, which you consider to be the more probable one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be quite a distance you're talking. About 3 degrees there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five degrees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five degrees [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The difference between 67 and 72 is 5, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be as much as 50, or in some cases even probably up to 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some cases would -- isn't it true that you look at the firing table that you get an answer and not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In some case this is, and in some cases that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You'll get a distance, a figure from the firing tables, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer was 50 or in some cases 100. I mean, what's -- if you say, I would have to look that up, that's a fair answer. But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the range tables there will be a set figure. In reality -- when you fire a mortar in reality, the distance actually could be smaller or greater, depending upon other factors. But in the range tables, they will give you a set figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, what I was looking for was what the average difference in distance would be. But perhaps if we look at the tables we could see whether the difference is 50 to 100 metres. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then you list charges. Charge number 1, 900 metres; charge 2, 1600 metres; charge 3, 2400; and charge 4, 3.000 metres. Well, I will have to start with charge 1, even though you said that this firing position was inside the perimeter of the confrontation line. But in order for you to understand further on, because I'm going ask you to make some markings in the tables, can we now move from your statement to 1D1293, which is the firing table. We don't have it in English, but we are going to deal with numbers mainly. Therefore, I think it won't be difficult to follow. So this is the firing table for a light mortar, 120-millimetre M74.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 58, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here, we can see the table for charge 1. In the first column it says in B/C/S, "Distance in metres." So please focus on the line which starts with 900. We can see here, and we'll find the same number later on in the table, the table angle of 1 over 6.000, and then below you can see the figure 1101, 66.5 degrees, which is less than 67, as had been found - is that right? - and the trajectory peak in metres is 522. As for the table angle or elevation of 1100 metres, that is the data. Have you had an opportunity to see this table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you allow me either to repeat reading that line and see what it actually is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps you could enquire with your expert whether the number 1100 would perhaps, where it is linked to 1 to 6.000, whether these are Russian or Warsaw Pact mills which would be equal to approximately 66 degrees --

utterances.text: 67, yeah.

utterances.text: -- well, more or less. If that would explain then we slowly start understanding --

utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... my next question would clarify, I think --

utterances.text: -- for me and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Mr. Higgs, do you agree with me that all the trajectories with an angle lower than the trajectory of 1100 mills, according to this nomenclature would have a descent angle less than 67 degrees and that a projectile with such a trajectory would have fallen or would have hit the building in the market-place and could have not ended up on the road in front of the market-place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with those angles where there -- the lower angles where the descent angle would be less than 67 degrees, it would have hit the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, this sketch shows rounds which, according to the UNPROFOR report, should have been caught by the radar. All of the calculated trajectories could -- should have been caught because they are all higher than 522 metres.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, the charge 2 vertex height is higher than that for charge 1. So, again, not knowing why, what happened to the Cymbeline, that -- it is higher than the previous vertex height for charge 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that case, we might agree that Mr. Bleakely was right when he said that each shelled fired with charge 2 would have been picked up by the radar beam; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is where the Cymbeline was pointing, and I don't have that information, but, yes, I think that is probably a correct assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is not an assumption, but it was a conclusion. You make an assumption. What you say is not knowing how the Cymbeline was oriented, then you can't say anything about it. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, you do not have technical knowledge about the Cymbeline system. So the two, Mr. Lukic, should make us cautious in asking the witness to support conclusions on matters of which he has no thorough knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If Mr. Lukic could just assist me. I'm just having trouble finding something again. The 522 metres in the UN report, which report is he referring to and what page? I'm just having trouble finding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we read P797, page 3 in English and also in B/C/S, under number 4, what we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, could you assist me whether the Cymbeline was at the same elevation as the firing point you suggest? Is that an assumption?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Okay. Then --

utterances.text: Only it's not my theory. It's the finding in a bit different way, by the UN, telling about these 900 metres.

utterances.text: So we just converted it into this chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.text: That's your theory.

utterances.text: I think it's calculation, not theory.

utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave that for another day.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Oh. Line 1 is drawn across -- I was asked to draw a line across at approximately 522 metres, so that's why it has been drawn across just above the -- the .05 line.

utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you would agree with me that the figure of 522 doesn't appear in the paragraph you indicated in the UN report; is that correct?

utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to make the record clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Higgs, in your report on page 24, or, rather, 23, for 2400 metres distance, you cited charge 3. Now, back to the tables, and I would like to show you page 61 which pertains to charge 3.

utterances.text: This is 1D1293.

utterances.text: Yes, I missed that part. Thank you.

utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.text: Document as marked by the witness receives number D404, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This will relate to the previous ones as well, but I omitted to ask you if it is correct that all the paths to the right, from the 1100 one, have a smaller angle of descent than 67 degrees.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they will have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, angle of firing, angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Angle of descent of 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is -- yes. But is what -- the 1100 line, is that reflecting the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That one is more than 67, so there is possibility that one -- that one and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. My question is: Is the 1100 line, is that reflecting the angle of firing or is it reflecting the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is basically in connection of angle of descent of -- with that 67 degrees. It has to have that angle at least to miss the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that. But what is the -- we are looking at the table. We are looking at a line reflecting ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The sketch. Yes, now -- I mean, the sketch related to the table at the line, which seems to reflect an 1100 indication, which I thought might be linked to an angle, and that's what you do as well. My single -- simple question is: Is it reflecting the angle of descent or is it reflecting the angle of firing?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That angle of firing changes, and I didn't show maybe because it might cause confusion because I was mostly focussed on this 67 degrees. And this 1100 is in connection of 67 degrees and more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 67 degrees is the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'm not saying that there's not a link or a relation between the angle of firing and the angle of descent, but the question is whether they are the same. Perhaps we could ask the witness. Is the angle of firing exactly the same or slightly different or considerably different from the angle of descent, if the shell lands at the same altitude as from where it was fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The angle of descent is slightly different from the angle of firing. This graph here, the 1100, does relate to the angle of firing. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to be clear on that, we can see page 58. That's table for second charge. This is first charge. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In theory, it should be the same. The angle of descent -- apparently because the horizontal speed diminishes during flight, the angle of descent will be steeper. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So I'm not saying there is no relation but what is reflected in the table, the 1100, seems to be the angle of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Resulting in a slightly steeper angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how I understand it and how witness explained it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 14297, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a report dated 8th September 1995 compiled by UNPROFOR. The Cymbeline radar operates 24 hours a day and was operating on the 28th of August, 1995, at the time of the mortar firing. The Cymbeline was fully operational and manned by an experienced crew who would have detected at least several of the mortars if they passed through the Cymbeline's radar beam. The Cymbeline crew did not detect any of the five mortars fired, however, was able to provide circumstantial information." And now it goes on to say that: "The high terrain partially blocked the line of sight of the Cymbeline radar dish; hence, the angle of the radar dish was fixed at a higher angle. At this angle, it detects mortars fired in a higher trajectory, but not in a lower trajectory." So what we see here that there were no obstacles to detect any shells flying above the indicated point. Did you bear in mind and did you take into consideration this UNPROFOR report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD HIGGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this report. Again, I don't know why it didn't detect any of the rounds. So I -- on my report it continued with the -- the evidence I had and therefore came to the -- the -- the conclusions I made in the reports.

utterances.text: You don't have the whole day tomorrow because we are not sitting [Overlapping speakers] ...
